title: Graph M-Coloring
excerpt: Color a graph so no two connected nodes match. The goal shifts from finding every answer to finding one, and that single change rewrites how the recursion returns.

content.text: Color every node of a graph so that no two connected nodes share a color, using at most
m
colors. It sounds like a puzzle and it is really a scheduling problem in disguise.

Exams that share students cannot run in the same slot. Radio towers that overlap cannot use the same frequency. Variables alive at the same moment cannot share a CPU register. In each case the things are nodes, the conflicts are edges, and the colors are the resource you are rationing.
Every problem so far in this section wanted
all
the answers. Subsets listed every subset, N-Queens counted all 92 solutions. Coloring usually wants
one
answer, or just a yes or no.

That changes the code in a way worth being deliberate about. When you are collecting everything, the recursive call returns nothing and the loop always continues to the next choice. When you want one answer, the recursive call returns a boolean, and a success has to stop the search and travel all the way back up through every caller.
In the template that means the explore step becomes a decision rather than a plain statement:
if (solve(...)) return true;
. Without that, the search finds a valid coloring and then cheerfully undoes it and keeps looking, which is both slow and confusing to debug.
Five regions and three colors, colored in a fixed order, is small enough to watch the whole run happen below without a single rejection.

This example is easy enough to need no backtracking at all, which is itself worth seeing: backtracking algorithms do not always backtrack. Drop to two colors and it becomes impossible, and the search has to exhaust every branch before it can say so.
That asymmetry is general. Proving something is possible means finding one example. Proving it is impossible means ruling out everything, which is usually far more expensive.
Color the graph yourself, then let the solver run. Reduce the number of colors until it fails and watch how much more work the failure costs than the success did.

There is redundancy in this search that is easy to miss. If you find a valid coloring, then swapping every red for green and every green for red gives another valid coloring. The colors have no meaning of their own, only their pattern of agreement and disagreement matters.

So the search wastes time exploring branches that are relabelings of each other. The standard fix is to insist that the first node always takes color 0, and more generally that a node may only use a new color if every lower-numbered color has already been used somewhere. That removes whole families of duplicate branches without losing a single genuinely distinct answer.
Symmetry breaking of this kind shows up all over search problems, and it is usually the largest available win after the basic prune.

body.text: Why there is no clever formula

content.text: It is fair to ask whether some direct method exists that avoids searching. For 2 colors, yes: a graph is 2-colorable exactly when it contains no odd-length cycle, and one traversal decides it.

From 3 colors upward, no efficient method is known. The problem is NP-complete, which in practice means that if you find a fast general algorithm for it you have solved one of the major open problems in computer science. Until then, search with good pruning is the honest answer, and knowing that saves you from hunting for a formula that probably does not exist.

It also explains why the four color theorem is famous. Every map drawn on a plane needs at most four colors, which is a strong statement about a specific family of graphs, and it took a computer-assisted proof to establish. General graphs have no such bound.
Ignoring the recursive call's return value.
The single most common bug in find-one-answer problems. The solver finds a coloring, discards it, and reports failure or takes far longer than it should.
Undoing after a success.
The undo belongs in the failure path only. If it runs after a successful return, the answer is dismantled on the way back up and the caller receives an empty result.
Checking neighbors that have no color yet.

Comparing against an unassigned node should never block a color. In languages where a missing key reads as a default value, an uncolored neighbor can accidentally match color 0 and rule it out everywhere.
Expecting a fast answer for large graphs.
No pruning makes this problem easy in general. If your input is large and arbitrary, look for structure in it or accept an approximate answer.

questions.prompt: Why does the recursive call return a boolean here when subsets returned nothing?

options.label: The goal is one answer rather than all of them, so a success must stop the search and propagate upward
Because coloring can fail and subsets cannot
To make the un-choose step unnecessary

questions.prompt: Where does the un-choose step belong in a find-one-answer search?

options.label: Only on the failure path, after the recursive call reports it did not work
Always, immediately after the recursive call

questions.prompt: Why does forcing the first node to color 0 lose no solutions?

options.label: Colors have no meaning individually, so any coloring can be relabeled to start with color 0
Because color 0 is always safe for the first node
Because the first node has the fewest neighbors

questions.prompt: Deciding 2-colorability is easy but 3-colorability is not. What is the 2-color test?

options.label: A graph is 2-colorable exactly when it has no odd-length cycle, which one traversal can check
It has fewer edges than nodes
